title: Aeolus, keeper of the winds
greek: Αἴολος Ἱπποτάδης, φίλος ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν (Aiolos Hippotadēs, philos athanatoisi theoisin) ... ταμίην ἀνέμων (tamiēn anemōn)
short: Aeolus is not yet the god of the winds of later myth but a mortal king, 'dear to the gods', whom Zeus has made 'steward' (tamiēs) of the winds.
body: Homer's Aeolus, son of Hippotas ('horseman'), lives a life of endless feasting with his wife and twelve children, the six sons married to the six daughters. This sibling marriage, unthinkable among Greeks, marks the island as a closed, self-sufficient fairy-tale world, like the Phaeacians' isolation. Zeus has made him tamiēs, 'steward, dispenser', of the winds (10.21), the same word used of a housekeeper who keeps the stores: he controls the winds as a householder controls provisions. He should be distinguished from Aeolus son of Hellen, ancestor of the Aeolians (named at 11.237 as father of Cretheus). Later poets made Aeolus a god ruling the winds in a cave (Virgil, Aeneid 1.52-63). Ancient geographers placed his island among the Lipari ('Aeolian') islands north of Sicily; Eratosthenes, quoted by Strabo, retorted that one would find the scene of Odysseus' wanderings when one found the cobbler who stitched the bag of winds.

title: The 'floating island'
greek: πλωτῇ ἐνὶ νήσῳ (plōtēi eni nēsōi)
short: Aeolus' island floats, ringed by a wall of unbreakable bronze and sheer cliffs: a drifting wonder that is hard to find twice.
body: Plōtos usually means 'floating' or 'navigable'. Merry and Riddell report that Aristarchus took it as 'drifting', whereas Crates read 'accessible to ships'; they prefer 'floating', comparing Pindar on the wandering island of Delos and Herodotus' story of the floating island of Chemmis in Egypt, and they rule out Crates' view because an island walled by sheer cliffs would be harbourless. They also offer a rationalising guess that sailors' tales of icebergs lie behind the image. Whatever its origin, the floating island suits the episode: Odysseus is carried back to it by chance (10.54-55), but it is no fixed place on a map. Compare the 'Wandering Rocks' (Planctae) at 12.61, another feature of the sea that refuses to stay still.

title: The bag of winds
greek: δῶκε δέ μ᾽ ἐκδείρας ἀσκὸν βοὸς ἐννεώροιο (dōke de m' ekdeiras askon boos enneōroio)
short: Aeolus binds the adverse winds in an ox-hide bag, leaving only the West Wind free; the crew open it in sight of Ithaca, thinking it holds treasure.
body: The askos is a leather sack of the kind used for wine (Odysseus brought Maro's wine to the Cyclops in one, 9.196). It is made from the hide of an ox 'nine years old', a formulaic age that marks size and vigour. With the contrary winds shut away, the West Wind carries the fleet eastward for nine days, until the coast of Ithaca and men tending fires are in sight. The crew's suspicion that it holds gold and silver links the disaster to the theme of shared spoils: they resent returning empty-handed while their leader is loaded with gifts (10.38-45). Nagy notes how the bag reverses direction: the free West Wind brings them east toward home; the escaped winds blow them back west, and from then on the voyage loses its bearings.

title: Odysseus' fatal sleep
greek: ἔνθ᾽ ἐμὲ μὲν γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἐπήλυθε κεκμηότα (enth' eme men glykys hypnos epēlythe kekmēota)
short: After nine days at the sheet, Odysseus falls asleep in sight of home, and the crew open the bag: the first of three crucial sleeps.
body: Odysseus had held the sheet, the rope controlling the sail, himself for nine days and nights, so that the return would be quick. Sleep overcomes him at the worst moment, and his men act behind his back. The same pattern is repeated on Thrinacia, where the gods 'shed sweet sleep upon my eyelids' while Eurylochus persuades the crew to kill the Sun's cattle (12.338, 12.372: 'pitiless sleep'). The third sleep is benign: Odysseus is carried home to Ithaca by the Phaeacians in a deep, death-like sleep (13.79-80). Sleep in the Odyssey thus marks the limits of the hero's control: when his vigilant mind is switched off, disaster or divine rescue takes over. His reaction here, debating whether to throw himself into the sea (10.49-53), is the nearest he comes to despair.

title: 'Our own folly'
greek: αὐτῶν γὰρ ἀπωλόμεθ᾽ ἀφραδίῃσιν (autōn gar apōlometh' aphradiēisin)
short: Odysseus' comment, given before he tells the story, makes the crew's thoughtlessness responsible for the disaster, echoing the poem's opening lines.
body: Aphradiē is 'thoughtlessness, lack of sense' (from a-, 'not', and phrazomai, 'consider'). The idea that humans bring suffering on themselves 'beyond their lot' is announced by Zeus in the first divine assembly of the poem (1.32-34), and the proem says that the companions perished 'through their own blind folly' (atasthaliai, 1.7) in eating the cattle of the Sun. Book 10 shows the pattern at work through the comrades' greed and suspicion. Note that Odysseus includes himself ('we were lost'), though he quickly blames 'my evil comrades and sleep accursed' when he returns to Aeolus (10.68-69). The narrator's moral judgement is part of the Apologoi's careful self-presentation.

title: Aeolus rejects a man 'hated of the gods'
greek: ἔρρ᾽ ἐκ νήσου θᾶσσον, ἐλέγχιστε ζωόντων ... ὅς κε θεοῖσιν ἀπέχθηται μακάρεσσιν (err' ek nēsou thasson, elenchiste zōontōn ... hos ke theoisin apechthētai makaressin)
short: When Odysseus returns, Aeolus drives him away: a man whose plans fail so spectacularly must be hated by the gods, and helping him would be impious.
body: The scene is a reversal of hospitality. Odysseus sits as a suppliant at the threshold (10.62-63), the place of the outcast, and asks for help 'with gentle words', but Aeolus reads misfortune as a sign of divine hostility and refuses to be involved. The logic is typical of archaic religion: success shows divine favour, failure divine anger, and it is dangerous to associate with someone the gods have rejected. Aeolus is the only host in the poem who sends a suppliant away, and his reasoning is not entirely wrong: Poseidon is in fact hostile to Odysseus, though Aeolus does not know it. The episode also marks a structural turn, as the windless rowing that follows exhausts the crew (10.78-79).

title: Lamus, Telepylus and the Laestrygonians
greek: Λάμου αἰπὺ πτολίεθρον, / Τηλέπυλον Λαιστρυγονίην (Lamou aipy ptoliethron, Tēlepylon Laistrygoniēn)
short: A city of cannibal giants with a perfect harbour, King Antiphates and a mountain-sized queen; eleven of Odysseus' twelve ships are destroyed there.
body: Lamus is either the founder-king of the city or the city itself; Merry and Riddell note that ancient poets (Horace, Ovid) treat Lamus as a person and connect the name with words for gullet and with the child-eating ogress Lamia. Telepylus means 'with far-off gates' or, as they prefer, 'big-gated'. The episode closely parallels the Cyclops: giant man-eaters, a reconnaissance party, a monstrous host. But it is far quicker and more brutal, with no trick and no escape for most; Odysseus survives only because he moored outside the harbour. The Laestrygonians are 'not like men but like the Giants' (10.120) and spear men 'like fishes' (10.124). Ancient tradition placed them in Sicily (Thucydides 6.2.1) or at Formiae in Italy (Horace, Odes 3.17).

anchor: could have earned a double wage
title: The land of the short nights
greek: ἔνθα κ᾽ ἄυπνος ἀνὴρ δοιοὺς ἐξήρατο μισθούς ... ἐγγὺς γὰρ νυκτός τε καὶ ἤματός εἰσι κέλευθοι (entha k' aypnos anēr doious exērato misthous ... engys gar nyktos te kai ēmatos eisi keleuthoi)
short: Night and day follow so closely that a sleepless herdsman could earn two wages; many readers have seen a memory of the far north's summer nights.
body: The 'paths of night and day are close together': the shepherd bringing his flock in at dusk meets the herdsman driving his cattle out at dawn. Crates of Mallos in antiquity related the lines to the constellation of the Dragon and to the very short nights of the north, and many modern readers see a sailors' report of northern latitudes, comparing Tacitus' account of the short night in northern Britain (Agricola 12). Merry and Riddell think Crates nearer the truth than the scholiasts' local explanations, but they also suggest that Homer imagines the sun's turning-point in the far west, where night is almost abolished, a wonder of the western 'wonder-land' rather than a northern report. The detail is in any case unique in Homer.

title: Laestrygonians 'like the Giants', men speared 'like fishes'
greek: οὐκ ἄνδρεσσιν ἐοικότες, ἀλλὰ Γίγασιν ... ἰχθῦς δ᾽ ὣς πείροντες (ouk andressin eoikotes, alla Gigasin ... ichthys d' hōs peirontes)
short: Two short comparisons turn the attack into a monstrous fishing raid: the giants spear Odysseus' men like fish and carry them home to eat.
body: The Gigantes in Homer are a savage race of the distant past (7.59-60 says Eurymedon king of the Giants destroyed his reckless people; 7.206 says the Phaeacians are close kin to the gods, as are the Cyclopes and the Giants). Later myth made them the earth-born rebels defeated by the Olympians in the Gigantomachy. The fishing simile reverses the normal relation of men to food: sailors who live by catching fish are themselves speared and eaten. The image looks forward to Scylla, who 'fishes' from her cave and pulls Odysseus' men up 'as a fisher on a jutting rock' lands a catch (12.251-255). Odysseus' crew, without supplies, are later forced to fish with bent hooks on Thrinacia (12.331-332).

title: Circe, daughter of Helios
greek: Κίρκη ἐϋπλόκαμος ... αὐτοκασιγνήτη ὀλοόφρονος Αἰήταο (Kirkē eüplokamos ... autokasignētē oloophronos Aiētao)
short: Circe is a goddess, child of the Sun and of Perse daughter of Ocean, and sister of Aeetes, king of Colchis in the Argonaut legend.
body: Homer introduces Circe with a genealogy: her father is Helios, her mother Perse, daughter of Oceanus, her brother Aeetes 'of baneful mind', the king from whom Jason took the Golden Fleece (the Argo is named at 12.70). Hesiod gives the same family (Theogony 956-957). This connection with the Argonaut story, set in the far east at Colchis, may explain why Circe's island lies at the 'risings of the sun' in 12.3-4, although the narrative seems to move westward. Merry and Riddell discuss both an eastern and a western Circe, the latter later placed at Monte Circeo in Italy. Ancient etymologists connected her name with kerkis, the weaver's shuttle, or with mixing (kirnēmi) potions; kirkos is also the Greek for a hawk, and Nagy suggests a link with krikos, 'circle'. Her island Aeaea ('land'?) is already mentioned at 9.32.

title: Lost bearings: 'where the darkness is or where the dawn'
greek: ὦ φίλοι, οὐ γάρ τ᾽ ἴδμεν ὅπῃ ζόφος οὐδ᾽ ὅπῃ ἠώς (ō philoi, ou gar t' idmen hopēi zophos oud' hopēi ēōs)
short: Odysseus admits that he cannot tell east from west and doubts whether any plan (mētis) is left to them: a low point for the man of many wiles.
body: Zophos, 'gloom', is the west and ēōs, 'dawn', the east (compare 9.26). The admission is remarkable on the lips of a hero whose identity rests on mētis: 'let us take thought if any device (mētis) be still left us. As for me I think not that there is' (10.192-193). Nagy connects this disorientation with the poem's link between nóos (mind, awareness) and nostos (return): losing one's sense of direction is losing the way home. The crew's reaction, remembering the Cyclops and Antiphates and weeping (10.198-202), shows the cumulative psychological effect of the earlier disasters. The speech also raises the geographical puzzle of Aeaea, an island whose location is explicitly beyond human orientation.

title: Eurylochus, the dissenting voice
greek: Εὐρύλοχος ἀντίθεος (Eurylochos antitheos)
short: Odysseus' kinsman and second-in-command, cautious at Circe's house and rebellious on Thrinacia, where his speech leads the crew to their death.
body: Eurylochus leads the half of the crew chosen by lot to scout Circe's house, and alone stays outside, suspecting a trap (10.232, 10.258). Back at the ship he refuses to return and later accuses Odysseus of 'folly' (atasthaliai) for the deaths in the Cyclops' cave (10.429-437); Odysseus nearly cuts off his head, 'near kinsman of mine by marriage though he was' (pēos, 10.441). Ancient tradition, followed in the scholia, made him the husband of Odysseus' sister Ctimene (15.363-364). In Book 12 his arguments win the crew over twice: to land on Thrinacia (12.278-293) and to eat the Sun's cattle (12.340-351). He thus embodies the opposite of Odysseus' endurance; yet some of his points are reasonable, and readers have often found him a sympathetic voice of the exhausted ordinary sailor.

title: Wolves and lions fawning like dogs
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἂν ἀμφὶ ἄνακτα κύνες δαίτηθεν ἰόντα / σαίνωσ᾽ (hōs d' hot' an amphi anakta kynes daitēthen ionta sainōs')
short: Circe's bewitched wolves and lions fawn on the visitors like dogs greeting a master home from dinner: a sinister sign of what her drugs do.
body: The beasts round Circe's house are, Homer says, made tame by her 'evil drugs' (kaka pharmaka, 10.213). They are often taken to be men she has transformed earlier, although Homer does not say so explicitly; Eurylochus later fears that she will make them 'swine, or wolves, or lions' (10.432-434), which suggests that this is how the crew understood it. The simile is domestic and comic (dogs wagging their tails for scraps), but the effect is unsettling, as wild predators behave like pets. The scene prepares for the transformation of the men into swine and recalls the dogs of Alcinous' palace, golden and silver guardians made by Hephaestus (7.91-94). It also contrasts with the loyal dog Argus in Book 17.

title: Circe at the loom, singing
greek: ἀειδούσης ὀπὶ καλῇ, / ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένης μέγαν ἄμβροτον (aeidousēs opi kalēi, histon epoichomenēs megan ambroton)
short: The men hear Circe singing as she weaves, exactly as Calypso was found by Hermes: weaving goddesses mark the dangerous, seductive women of the poem.
body: Walking to and fro before an upright loom while singing is what Calypso is doing when Hermes reaches Ogygia (5.61-62). Weaving was the central skill of Greek women, and in the Odyssey it is also a figure for cunning: Penelope's great web, woven by day and unravelled by night, keeps the suitors at bay (2.94-110). Circe's song is a lure, a first version of the danger of the Sirens' song in Book 12. Polites, 'dearest and trustiest' of Odysseus' comrades, cannot tell whether the singer is 'a goddess or a woman' (10.228), a phrase that recalls Odysseus' own flattering question to Nausicaa (6.149). Circe's web is 'imperishable' (ambrotos), the work of a goddess.

title: Circe's potion and Pramnian wine
greek: ἐν δέ σφιν τυρόν τε καὶ ἄλφιτα καὶ μέλι χλωρὸν / οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ ἐκύκα (en de sphin tyron te kai alphita kai meli chlōron oinōi Pramneiōi ekyka)
short: Circe stirs cheese, barley meal and honey into Pramnian wine: a kykeōn, a 'mixed drink', laced with drugs.
body: The verb ekyka ('stirred, mixed') gives the drink its name, kykeōn (10.290, 316). In the Iliad Hecamede prepares the same mixture, with grated goat's cheese and barley in Pramnian wine, to restore the wounded Machaon and Nestor (Il. 11.638-641), and a kykeōn of barley and mint is the ritual drink of the Eleusinian Mysteries (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 208-210). Merry and Riddell describe it as a thick restorative, more like a gruel than a drink. The origin of Pramnian wine was disputed in antiquity (Icaria, Smyrna, Lesbos); later writers describe it as dark and harsh. Circe's version is a hospitable drink turned into a weapon by the addition of pharmaka, 'drugs', so that the men 'utterly forget their native land' (10.236), the same danger as the lotus.

title: Swine with human minds
greek: οἱ δὲ συῶν μὲν ἔχον κεφαλὰς φωνήν τε τρίχας τε / καὶ δέμας, αὐτὰρ νοῦς ἦν ἔμπεδος ὡς τὸ πάρος περ (hoi de syōn men echon kephalas phōnēn te trichas te kai demas, autar nous ēn empedos hōs to paros per)
short: Struck by Circe's wand, the men become pigs in body and voice, but their nous, their mind, stays as it was, so they weep in the sty.
body: The transformation affects everything physical: head, voice, bristles and shape. Only the nous remains 'steadfast' (empedos), the same word Circe uses of Teiresias' mind, which alone survives death intact (10.493-494). The horror of the episode lies in this split: the men understand their state. Their food is acorns, mast and cornel-berries. Ancient readers allegorised the scene as men degraded by pleasure into beasts, with Odysseus' reason (and Hermes' moly) as the cure. Plutarch turned it round in his dialogue Gryllus ('Grunter'), in which one of the pigs argues that animals live more virtuously than humans and refuses to be changed back. When Circe restores them, they become 'younger than they were before, and far comelier and taller' (10.395-396).

title: Hermes disguised as a young man
greek: νεηνίῃ ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς, / πρῶτον ὑπηνήτῃ, τοῦ περ χαριεστάτη ἥβη (neēniēi andri eoikōs, prōton hypēnētēi, tou per chariestatē hēbē)
short: Hermes meets Odysseus disguised as a youth with his first beard, in lines that repeat his appearance to Priam in Iliad 24.
body: The description, 'a young man with the first down upon his lip, in whom the charm of youth is fairest', is identical to the lines describing Hermes when he meets Priam on the way to Achilles' hut (Il. 24.347-348). In both scenes Hermes is the guide who helps a mortal enter a dangerous dwelling and come out alive. He carries his golden wand (chrysorrapis) and is called Argeiphontes (10.302, 331), whose meaning was already uncertain in antiquity ('slayer of Argus' or 'bright-shining'). Hermes is the god of boundaries, travellers and cunning, and is the great-grandfather of Odysseus through Autolycus (19.395-398), so it is fitting that he helps him. As in the Iliad, a divine helper is necessary for a mortal to survive a goddess.

title: Moly, the herb of the gods
greek: μῶλυ δέ μιν καλέουσι θεοί· χαλεπὸν δέ τ᾽ ὀρύσσειν / ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι (mōly de min kaleousi theoi; chalepon de t' oryssein andrasi ge thnētoisi)
short: The magic herb Hermes gives Odysseus: black at the root, milk-white in flower, hard for mortals to dig, and known only by its name in the gods' language.
body: Moly protects Odysseus against Circe's drug. Homer sometimes gives a thing two names, one used by gods and one by men (e.g. Il. 1.403, Briareus/Aegaeon; 14.291, chalkis/kymindis); moly has only the divine name, because men do not know the plant. Merry and Riddell list attempts at identification (a kind of garlic, wild rue, hellebore) and report that Theophrastus knew a 'moly' growing in Arcadia used against spells (Enquiry into Plants 9.15.7), while preferring the view that it is the poet's invention. They note an old interpretation of chalepon as 'dangerous' rather than 'difficult' to dig, as with the mandrake. Allegorical readers, ancient and modern, took moly as reason or education, which protects against the bestial life Circe offers.

title: The oath and the danger of being 'unmanned'
greek: μή σ᾽ ἀπογυμνωθέντα κακὸν καὶ ἀνήνορα θήῃ (mē s' apogymnōthenta kakon kai anēnora thēēi)
short: Before sharing Circe's bed Odysseus must make her swear 'a great oath' not to harm him, lest she leave him 'unmanned' once he is naked.
body: Anēnōr literally means 'un-manned', deprived of manly strength (anēr). Behind Hermes' warning lies a widespread belief that love with a goddess is perilous for a mortal: in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (188-190) Anchises begs the goddess not to leave him 'strengthless' after their union. The oath is the standard device in Homer for binding a god (compare Calypso's oath at 5.178-187, sworn by Earth, Sky and the Styx). The scene inverts the normal power relation: Odysseus threatens Circe with a sword, she clasps his knees as a suppliant, and only after her oath does he consent. The sexual relationship is presented without moral comment; it lasts a year and becomes the basis of Circe's help.

title: Polytropos: the word of the first line
greek: ἦ σύ γ᾽ Ὀδυσσεύς ἐσσι πολύτροπος (ē sy g' Odysseus essi polytropos)
short: Circe recognises Odysseus with polytropos, 'of many turns', the epithet of the poem's first line, used of him only here and in 1.1.
body: Polytropos can mean 'much-travelled', 'turned many ways' by fortune, or 'versatile, wily', the man of many turns of mind; Murray chooses 'of ready device' here (and 'of many devices' for polymēchanos elsewhere). Its rarity makes this moment special: the goddess names Odysseus with the very word the poet used in the proem (1.1). Nagy interprets polytropos as 'turning into many different selves', comparing Hermes, the shape-shifting god who also bears the epithet in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes (line 13). Circe has been told of Odysseus' coming by Hermes (10.330-332), another instance of the prophecy fulfilled that runs through these books, as in Polyphemus' recognition of the man foretold by Telemus (9.507-512).

anchor: as when calves in a farmstead
title: The calves and the returning cows
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἂν ἄγραυλοι πόριες περὶ βοῦς ἀγελαίας ... σκαίρωσιν (hōs d' hot' an agrauloi porties peri bous agelaias ... skairōsin)
short: The men left at the ship crowd round Odysseus like calves frisking round their mothers coming home; to them it is as if they had reached Ithaca.
body: The simile transfers a homely farm scene to the beach of a strange island: the men are calves, Odysseus is the mother-cow returning from pasture, and the sudden joy is so great that 'it seemed to their hearts as though they had got to their native land'. Homer then makes the comparison explicit in the men's own words (10.419-420). The image of homecoming in the middle of the wanderings is poignant, since none of these men will ever reach Ithaca. It also prepares the emotional reunion in Circe's hall (10.453-454), and the far greater recognition scenes in Ithaca, in particular the simile of shipwrecked sailors reaching land that describes Penelope's joy (23.233-240).

title: Daimonie, 'strange man'
greek: δαιμόνι᾽, ἤδη νῦν μιμνήσκεο πατρίδος αἴης (daimoni', ēdē nyn mimnēskeo patridos aiēs)
short: After a year of feasting the men remind Odysseus of home, addressing him as daimonie, a vocative of surprise or gentle reproach.
body: Daimonios is derived from daimōn, 'divine power', and as a form of address it suggests that the person addressed is behaving as if under some strange influence. It ranges from affection to sharp rebuke: Hector and Andromache use it tenderly to each other (Il. 6.407, 486), while Zeus uses it impatiently to Hera (Il. 1.561). Here the crew gently scold their leader for forgetting the return. The reversal is notable: in the Lotus-eaters episode Odysseus dragged forgetful men back to the ships, and now it is the crew who remember nostos. The 'full year' (10.467-470) of enjoyment with Circe has no moral comment from the narrator, but it shows that even Odysseus can lose his bearings.

title: 'Dread Persephone', queen of the dead
greek: ἐπαινὴ Περσεφόνεια (epainē Persephoneia)
short: Persephone, wife of Hades, rules the dead with him; her standing epithet epainē means 'dread', and she controls which ghosts come and go.
body: Epainē is an old word, used only of Persephone in Homer; ancient grammarians explained it as 'dread' (as if equivalent to ainē) and some as 'praised'. In the Odyssey Persephone is the active power of the underworld: she grants Teiresias his intelligence (10.494-495), she 'sends forth' the women of the catalogue and scatters them (11.226, 385-386), and Odysseus fears she may send the Gorgon's head at him (11.634-635). Her groves of poplar and willow stand at the edge of the world (10.509-510). The myth of her abduction by Hades, told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, is not mentioned by Homer, who calls her 'daughter of Zeus' (11.217). Her name, of uncertain meaning, appears in many forms (Persephassa, Phersephatta).

title: Teiresias, the seer whose mind survives
greek: ψυχῇ χρησομένους Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο, / μάντηος ἀλαοῦ, τοῦ τε φρένες ἔμπεδοί εἰσι (psychēi chrēsomenous Thēbaiou Teiresiao, mantēos alaou, tou te phrenes empedoi eisi)
short: Circe sends Odysseus to consult the blind Theban seer, who alone among the dead keeps his understanding, granted by Persephone.
body: Teiresias was the great prophet of Thebes, a figure of Theban epic and later tragedy (Sophocles' Oedipus the King and Antigone, Euripides' Bacchae). Circe explains the reason for the journey: he 'alone' has phrenes empedoi, 'steadfast wits', while 'the others flit about as shadows' (skiai aïssousin, 10.495). This is the clearest statement of the Homeric view that the dead are mindless shades, a view Achilles' ghost will confirm (11.475-476). Nagy notes that Teiresias' nóos becomes active when he has drunk the sacrificial blood. Why Odysseus needs Teiresias is a well-known puzzle: Circe herself gives the detailed sailing directions in Book 12. Teiresias' real contribution is a vision of Odysseus' life beyond the poem, including his death (11.100-137).

title: Persephone's groves: poplars and 'fruit-losing' willows
greek: μακραί τ᾽ αἴγειροι καὶ ἰτέαι ὠλεσίκαρποι (makrai t' aigeiroi kai iteai ōlesikarpoi)
short: On the far shore of Oceanus stand Persephone's groves of tall poplars and willows that lose their fruit: trees of barrenness for the realm of death.
body: Ōlesikarpos, 'fruit-destroying' (ollymi + karpos), is unique in Homer. Merry and Riddell quote Pliny the Elder, who says the willow sheds its seed before it ripens and that Homer therefore called it frugiperda, 'fruit-losing'; an ancient scholiast adds that barren things belong to the dead. Circe's directions give a full underworld geography for the first time in Greek literature: a 'level shore' (akte lacheia) beyond the stream of Oceanus, the groves, and then the meeting of the rivers. In Odysseus' own account in Book 11 the scene is simpler, and he never seems to cross into Hades itself.

title: Oceanus, the river round the world
greek: δι᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο περήσῃς (di' Ōkeanoio perēsēis)
short: Oceanus is not the sea but a great river encircling the flat disc of the earth; the land of the dead lies on its far side.
body: In Homeric cosmology the earth is surrounded by the river Okeanos, 'deep-flowing' and 'back-flowing' (apsorrhoos), from which all rivers and springs come (Il. 21.195-197); it is pictured on the rim of Achilles' shield (Il. 18.607-608). The sun and stars rise from it and set in it. To reach the dead, Odysseus must sail to the end of the world and cross or travel along this river; in Book 11 he beaches the ship beside it in the land of the Cimmerians (11.13-22). Nagy stresses that Oceanus marks the boundary of the cosmos, beyond which the sun does not shine. Anticleia tells Odysseus that no living man can cross it on foot (11.157-159). Oceanus is also a god, father of Perse, Circe's mother (10.139).

title: The rivers of the underworld
greek: ἔνθα μὲν εἰς Ἀχέροντα Πυριφλεγέθων τε ῥέουσιν / Κώκυτός θ᾽, ὃς δὴ Στυγὸς ὕδατός ἐστιν ἀπορρώξ (entha men eis Acheronta Pyriphlegethōn te rheousin Kōkytos th', hos dē Stygos hydatos estin aporrhōx)
short: Fiery Pyriphlegethon and Cocytus, the 'river of wailing', a branch of the Styx, flow into Acheron at a rock where Odysseus must dig his pit.
body: These are the first named rivers of the Greek underworld. The names are expressive: Pyriphlegethōn (Murray 'Periphlegethon') is 'blazing with fire', Kōkytos comes from kōkyō, 'wail', and Acheron was linked by ancient etymologists with achos, 'grief'. The Styx, 'the hateful', is the river by which the gods swear their most binding oath (5.185-186). There was a real river Acheron in Thesprotia in north-west Greece, with a famous oracle of the dead (Nekyomanteion) near its mouth, mentioned by Herodotus (5.92); it is possible that Homer's geography draws on such a cult place. Later poets developed the system, most fully Virgil in Aeneid 6, where Charon ferries souls across, and Dante.

title: The rite for summoning the dead
greek: βόθρον ὀρύξαι ... ἀμφ᾽ αὐτῷ δὲ χοὴν χεῖσθαι πᾶσιν νεκύεσσι (bothron oryxai ... amph' autōi de choēn cheisthai pasin nekyessi)
short: Circe prescribes a pit, libations of milk-and-honey, wine and water, barley meal, vows, and the blood of a black ram and ewe turned toward Erebus.
body: The ritual combines elements of offerings to the dead and to the gods of the underworld: a bothros (pit) rather than a raised altar, choai (poured libations) for all the dead, and black victims whose heads are turned down toward Erebus, the dark realm below, while Odysseus looks away toward the river. The promised sacrifices at home, a barren heifer for the dead and a black ram for Teiresias, follow the logic of offering to the dead things that will not reproduce. The blood in the pit is the key: the shades must drink it to recover speech and recognition, so Odysseus guards it with his sword. Nagy discusses the bothros and the choē, and notes small differences between Circe's instructions and their performance in 11.23-50.

title: 'The powerless heads of the dead'
greek: νεκύων ἀμενηνὰ κάρηνα (nekyōn amenēna karēna)
short: A formula for the ghosts: they are 'heads' without menos, the vital force or mental energy of the living.
body: Amenēnos means 'without menos', the surge of strength and spirit that drives a living hero. Karēna, 'heads', stands for persons, as in the Iliadic phrase about souls of heroes sent to Hades (Il. 11.55, 'many strong heads'). Nagy translates 'skulls' and suggests the image of heads empty of mental power. The phrase recurs at 10.536 and 11.29 and 11.49 and fits Circe's statement that only Teiresias keeps his wits. Homer's dead are thus not punished or rewarded souls in the later sense, but dim, enfeebled copies of the living; only the 'Great Sinners' passage later in Book 11 shows personal punishment.

title: Elpenor's fall
greek: Ἐλπήνωρ δέ τις ἔσκε νεώτατος (Elpēnōr de tis eske neōtatos)
short: The youngest of the crew, sleeping off wine on Circe's roof, forgets the ladder and breaks his neck: an unheroic death that will demand a heroic burial.
body: Homer introduces Elpenor with unusual frankness: 'not over valiant in war nor sound of understanding'. His death is accidental, caused by wine and confusion, and the crew leave in such haste that no one notices; he will be the first ghost Odysseus meets (11.51-83). The name may suggest elpis, 'hope', with an ironic ring. The episode has a structural purpose, linking Circe's island and the underworld: Elpenor's request for burial forces Odysseus back to Aeaea (12.8-15), where Circe gives the sailing directions. Nagy points out that this is the beginning of a sequence connected with Odysseus' own homecoming. The image of the young man on the roof also gave later poets a figure of pathetic waste (e.g. Elpenor in Ezra Pound's first Canto).

anchor: Who with his eyes could behold
title: Gods who pass unseen
greek: τίς ἂν θεὸν οὐκ ἐθέλοντα / ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδοιτ᾽ ἢ ἔνθ᾽ ἢ ἔνθα κιόντα; (tis an theon ouk ethelonta ophthalmoisin idoit' ē enth' ē entha kionta?)
short: Circe has already tethered the black ram and ewe by the ship without being seen: the book ends with a reflection on how gods move among men.
body: The rhetorical question closes the book on a note of mystery. Homeric gods appear to mortals in disguise (Hermes as a young man earlier in this book, Athena as Mentor or a Phaeacian girl), and they may also act unseen, as Circe does here. A god is seen only when the god wishes. The idea recurs in Odysseus' meeting with Athena on Ithaca, where he tells her that she is hard to recognise for a mortal, however knowing, because she takes every shape (13.312-313). The sacrificial animals, provided by the goddess, show that the journey to the dead is sanctioned and planned by her, even as the crew weep and tear their hair at the news.
